related_questions.question: How accurate are home COVID tests?

text_blocks.snippet: Home COVID-19 tests, also known as rapid antigen tests, are generally accurate in detecting the presence of the virus when a person is infected, but they are less reliable at ruling out infection, especially early in the course of illness or in people without symptoms. While positive results are typically accurate, negative results may be false, particularly if symptoms are present or close contact with a confirmed case has occurred.
snippet_highlighted_words: generally accurate in detecting the presence of the virus when a person is infected

list.title: Positive results are generally reliable:
list.snippet: If a home test shows a positive result, it's highly likely that the individual is infected with COVID-19.

list.title: Negative results may be less reliable:
list.snippet: A negative result on a rapid antigen test, especially when symptoms are present or close contact has occurred, should not be taken as definitive proof of not being infected.

list.title: False negatives are possible:
list.snippet: Antigen tests, like those used in home tests, may not detect the virus early in the infection or in people who have no symptoms.

list.title: Follow-up testing may be needed:
list.snippet: When a negative result is obtained on a home test, especially if symptoms are present or close contact has occurred, it's recommended to repeat the test or follow up with a molecular test (like a PCR test), which is more sensitive.

list.title: Testing frequency:
list.snippet: If you are in close contact with someone who has tested positive for COVID-19 and you are experiencing symptoms, you should test yourself, even if your first test is negative.

list.title: Symptoms matter:
list.snippet: If you are feeling sick, even with a negative test result, you should assume you may have COVID-19 and isolate yourself to protect others.
